Core keyword census: MUST 81 to 68, MUST NOT 26 to 24, SHOULD 5 to 1, MAY 3 to 2; every difference is a moved occurrence. Core body 11,250 to about 10,000 words.

## Other drafts

* **Registration** keeps its own expiry and renewal rules, including later-`iat` replacements and atomic updates, and depends on the core alone. Withdrawal of the governing statement and global supersession are extension behavior; an earlier-`iat` statement at the token or pushed authorization request endpoint, and in a repeated public-client registration, is rejected by registration's own rules.
* **Lifecycle** (renamed from status): lifecycle semantics (withdrawal, supersession, currency on refresh, refresh replacement, errors), then the Token Status List and Shared Signals text as Status Mechanisms with anchors kept. Renewal and replacement require neither mechanism.

No sentence promises lifecycle behavior as core behavior.

Their other findings are the last eight commits; the fix commits got a normative diff against the reviewed tree and a separate reader.

pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Following #112: core keeps only what core processes. Seven passages in core served only registration or lifecycle. Each is either deleted, where the extension already says it, or moved there. One commit per item. No requirement keyword changes in any draft.

## Changes

| # | Core text | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `statement_uses` (3): "A delivery renewing a registration is a `registration` use" and "as is a refresh replacement under LIFECYCLE" | First moves to registration's Renewal, next to where a delivery is defined. Second deleted: lifecycle 5.2 already says a refresh replacement "is a `presentation` use". |
| 2 | 7.1 `statement_required`: "also applies when a statement delivered ... under REGISTRATION does not satisfy the requirements for a replacement" | Deleted; registration's Error Responses already assigns the code. Now reads "An extension such as {{REGISTRATION}} or {{LIFECYCLE}} can assign it to further cases." |
| 3 | 7.1 heading "Requiring a Current Statement" | Renamed "Statement Required Error". The old heading repeated lifecycle 5.1's, though 7.1 only defines the code. Anchor and number unchanged. |

pulls.title: Restructure Pulled Statements
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Section 5.5 was hard to follow. It opened with a metadata definition and HTTP rules, never said how a pull differs from a presentation, and its binding rules were repeated in 5.6, 5.6.2 and 5.6.3. This PR restructures it and keeps one home for each rule.

## New outline

```
5.5   Pulled Statements        lead: how a pull differs from a presentation;
                               software_statements_uri; metadata pointer
5.5.1 Retrieval and Selection  HTTP rules, which statements count, which one
                               applies, what happens when none does
5.5.2 Binding                  the table, now the single home for pulled
                               binding and pulled review-only cases
```

The lead states the three differences: the server chooses the statement; a pull that yields nothing leaves the request as if no statement were presented; and a pulled statement is review-only in the cases 5.5.2 identifies.

## Commits

1. **Restructure (editorial):**
   * The text moves under the lead and the two subsections.
   * The ordering sentence becomes "the ordering of step 2 of Section 5.1 applies only to the retrievals that follow".
   * "keeps only the latest `iat` from each issuer and applies any one of those" becomes "the most recently issued statement from an issuer of its choice" (same rule).
   * Restatements of 5.6 and 5.7 are dropped and the table cells shortened. The case of a document that omits `token_endpoint_auth_method` joins the table.
   * Citations about binding and failed pulls point at the new subsections.
2. **Single home (editorial):** 5.6 and 5.6.2 drop their pulled-statement sentences. 5.6.3 items 2 to 4 become "A pulled statement that Section 5.5.2 makes review-only."
3. **Withdrawal note dropped:** "A retrieval failure is never a withdrawal ({{LIFECYCLE}})". Core defines no withdrawal.
4. **Clarification:** with a required issuer, the server filters out other issuers' statements and applies the required issuer's most recently issued one. Before, "that issuer's statement" did not say which one when it published several.
5. **Clarification:** the MAY now names when a server may pull: a request opening a new grant at the token endpoint, the pushed authorization request endpoint, or the authorization endpoint. It used to read as any request whose client document is resolved, including code redemption and refresh, which the binding table and the 5.3 failure exception did not cover. Lifecycle defines pulling on refresh itself.
6. **Lifecycle:** both citations of core 5.5 (selection under the `iat` floor, and pulling on refresh) now cite 5.5.1.
7. **MCP profile:** its pull trigger follows item 5 ("when the client opens a new grant without presenting a statement").
8. **Review fix:** the lead's third bullet now reads "A pulled statement is review-only in the cases Section 5.5.2 identifies." The earlier wording ("cannot bind") read broader than 5.5.2, since a confidential client whose authentication fails is still rejected.

## Normative changes

Items 4 and 5 are the only intended changes in meaning. No keyword is added or removed (core census unchanged: MUST 68, MUST NOT 24, MAY 2). The keyword order differs only because the MAY now precedes the `software_statements_uri` definition.

## Verification

pulls.title: Admit presentation on any token request that opens a grant
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Token Endpoint (5.4.1) allowed a presentation only on client credentials and the assertion grants, or on a grant whose own specification provides for it. That excluded token exchange, which ID-JAG clients use at the IdP, the place where an enterprise IdP decides whether this software may get an ID-JAG. Neither RFC 8693 nor ID-JAG will opt in to this draft, so the escape hatch never applied.

The restriction existed (commit `b0c220f`) to keep presentation off a grant whose resource owner can approve the client before any statement is checked. This PR states that principle instead of a list.

## Change

> At the token endpoint, a runtime presentation is valid on a request that opens a new grant in that request, such as one using the `client_credentials` grant, the JWT or SAML 2.0 assertion grant (Section 2.1 of {{RFC7523}} and Section 2.1 of {{RFC7522}}), or token exchange {{RFC8693}}.
>
> It is not valid on a request that continues or completes a grant an earlier request began, such as authorization-code redemption, refresh-token use ({{grant-lifecycle}}, {{refresh}}), or redemption of a device code {{RFC8628}}. Admission belongs to the request that begins the grant, before the resource owner approves the client.

* **Extension Points:** the bullet changes from "grants other than those Token Endpoint names, such as token exchange" to "the request that begins a grant at an endpoint this specification does not cover, such as the device authorization endpoint of RFC 8628".
* **References:** RFC 8628 and RFC 8693 are added as informative.

## Normative change

* **Broadened:** token exchange, and any grant that opens in a single token request, now accepts a runtime presentation without its specification opting in. The "grant whose specification provides for it" clause is gone, because the principle covers it.
* **Exclusions:** a presentation on a grant that an earlier request began is still invalid. Code redemption and refresh are excluded as before, device code redemption is named, and what happens to a `software_statement` parameter in those requests is unchanged (5.4, 5.7).
* **No other rule is needed for token exchange:**
  * client authentication binds a confidential client;
  * public clients are already rejected at the token endpoint (5.6.2);
  * the reviewed metadata caps `grant_types`;
  * 5.4 already forbids `software_statement` on a token exchange that asks for a statement to be issued (issuance's Token Exchange Profile).
* No keyword is added or removed (core keyword sequence identical, 85 to 85).

## Verification

All five drafts build, and each draft's idnits counts are unchanged (core 4 warnings and 3 comments, registration 3 and 3). No rendered line is over 72 columns, there are no em dashes, and `git diff --check` is clean. No anchors are lost or added. No other draft cites the old grant list.

pulls.title: Clarify Error Responses for authorization requests
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Section 7.4, "Authorization Endpoint", read like a protocol section rather than part of Error Responses. It repeated the heading of 5.4.2, and its first paragraph packed two codes and their shared condition into one sentence.

2. **Codes as a list:** 7.4 now leads with the shared condition and lists each code, as 7.2 does:

   > If the authorization server's policy or a required issuer requires reviewed software, an authorization request from a client the server has not admitted on a statement is rejected in the authorization error response (Section 4.1.2.1 of RFC 6749) with the following error codes:
   >
   > `unauthorized_client`: The client is review-only, or a required issuer excludes the software from the tenant.
   >
   > `temporarily_unavailable`: A pull of statements, or the retrieval of a statement key set needed to verify a pulled statement, did not complete.

   The redirect paragraph and the `software_statement` paragraph are unchanged.

## Normative change

pulls.title: Simplify Error Responses
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Section 7 kept its request-by-request layout but repeated shared rules in every subsection and mixed formats. This PR states each shared rule once and lists every code. Section numbers are unchanged.

## Changes

1. **Precedence stated once in the lead of Section 7.** A rejection for a reason this specification defines uses the first of these that applies:
   1. `invalid_request`, for `software_statement` in a role 5.4 does not permit;
   2. `temporarily_unavailable`, for a retrieval that did not complete, including a pull or the key set needed to verify a pulled statement, and never the size bound;
   3. the code that 7.2, 7.3, or 7.4 assigns.

   The SHOULD 503, the "another reason uses the grant's own code" rule (now with both examples), and the extension sentence also sit in the lead. These replace:
   * the `temporarily_unavailable` clauses in the leads of 7.2 and 7.3, and the entry in 7.4;
   * the `invalid_request` paragraph of 7.4 ("in place of any other code");
   * the "another reason" and extension sentences in 7.2 and 7.3.
2. **7.2:** the `unauthorized_client` entry is four bullets, like `invalid_client`, instead of one run-on sentence. Its precedence over `statement_required` leads the entry.
3. **7.3:** code redemption's codes are a list, like refresh's. Its `invalid_request` for carrying a statement is covered by rule 1.
4. **7.4:** the two redirect paragraphs become one, covering every error at the authorization endpoint: validate `redirect_uri` against the CIMD (or a registered client's URIs) before redirecting, and never redirect if the CIMD can't be resolved.
5. **Citations:** lifecycle ("as Section 7.3 provides" for `temporarily_unavailable`) and registration ("as Section 7.4 provides" for `invalid_request`) now cite Section 7.

## Normative change

* **Gap closed:** code redemption now gets `temporarily_unavailable` for a retrieval that did not complete. One case is the `jwks_uri` of a confidential client whose statement was pulled at the authorization endpoint. Before, it had no code. This was on the -01 list.
* **No other change in meaning.** Rule 1 before rule 2 matches existing behavior: a wrong-role `software_statement` is detected without any retrieval, and 7.4 already put `invalid_request` ahead of every other code. The keyword sequence is identical (85 to 85), and no keyword sentence newly leads a paragraph.

## Verification

* Section 7 shrinks from about 940 to 879 words. No anchors are lost or added.

After a refresh, core cites -05, and -05 still defines `aud_tenant` (Section 3.1) and registers it (Section 11.5). Core cites no ID-JAG section numbers. CI builds with fresh references.

pulls.title: Editorial pass on core and registration before -00
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Full editorial pass on core and registration before -00, after this week's restructuring. Four cold reviewers produced findings: a working-group reviewer, an implementer, an RFC editor (simplification and polish), and a registration reviewer. I added my own read, triaged everything into one plan, and you approved all 13 clarifications and the Section 6 move. One commit per finding, so any can be dropped alone. Two cold verifiers then checked every commit against its base. Their 14 findings are the last 14 commits.

## Normative changes

**Contradictions fixed**
* **Pulled versus presented** (all three core reviewers). Section 2 counts a pulled statement as a runtime presentation. As a result, 5.6, 5.6.2 and the matching 6.2 `invalid_client` case rejected the very cases the 5.5.2 table makes review-only. Those rejections now apply to "a presentation made in a request" and point to 5.5.2.
* **5.6.2 scope.** The public-client binding list applied only at the pushed authorization request endpoint, although 5.5.2 sends authorization-endpoint pulls to it. The lead now covers both.
* **Registration, public-client re-registration.** One request was both "answered with the existing registration" (MUST) and "renewed or rejected". Now the server MUST NOT create another registration, and the outcome follows `iat`:
  * the same statement gets the existing registration;
  * a later one is evaluated as a delivery;
  * an earlier one is rejected.
  
  A public-client request meeting none of these, such as one in another tenant, is processed as a new registration. The text did not cover that case before. A later statement confined to a tenant, sent where an unrestricted registration is usable, is evaluated as a delivery and rejected by its tenant rules. Before, it would have created a second registration.
* **Registration digest.** Registration restated core 5.2 but omitted its "retrieve once more if held octets mismatch" rule. It now compares as core 5.2 requires and still rejects on a mismatch.

**Clarifications**
* 3.2 checks that `kid` is present. Section 3 already requires it.
* 6.2: `statement_required` applies when expiry is the statement's only validation failure. Otherwise the code is `invalid_client`.
* 5.2 and registration: omitted `grant_types` and `response_types` take their RFC 7591 defaults.
* 6.4: the authorization request `statement_required` MUST is anchored to Section 6's precedence.
* 5.7: the code redemption rules apply to codes bound to an establishment. Review-only presentations have none.

**Tightened**
* **One statement key set rule for every issuer** (Section 4; Section 8 points to it): the issuer MUST NOT publish a statement key in any other JWK Set. For an authorization server issuer, this now covers every JWK Set it publishes, such as a Status List key set. Before, the restriction covered only its `jwks_uri`.

**Moved between drafts (same force)**
* **To issuance.** Core's MUST NOT on carrying `software_statement` in an *issuance* request becomes an entry in issuance's Prohibited Parameters. The core defines no issuance request.
* **To lifecycle.** Five registration rules move into lifecycle:
  * a refusal record ending a registration;
  * the SHOULD to consult a withdrawal mechanism at each token request;
  * the governing statement staying current after the `iat` floor rises;
  * renewal counting toward the floor;
  * rejecting a delivery below the floor.
  
  Registration now says a registration is valid until its governing statement ceases to be current, which the core already defines to cover an extension ending it. This stays one-way: a lifted refusal does not revive the registration, so only a valid replacement does. A superseded statement keeps its `invalid_software_statement` code, and lifecycle rejects only *replacements* below the floor. The governing statement and the repeated statement in an RFC 7592 update still proceed.

**Keyword census**
* **Core:** MUST 68 to 64 and MUST NOT 24 to 21. These come from Section 8's duplicate key rules (now in Section 4), the issuance MUST NOT moving out, and the `aud_tenant` MUST splitting in two.
* **Registration:** MUST 29 to 28 and SHOULD 4 to 3. These come from the merged digest bullets, the re-registration rewrite, the RFC 6749 redirect restatement, the SHOULD moving to lifecycle, and a new explicit MUST to reject duplicate member names. That last one restores a reach the core rule used to have.
* **Lifecycle:** unchanged at 57. The SHOULD joined an existing sentence.

## Editorial

* **Leftovers from the split:**
  * Lifecycle restatements are trimmed from the core.
  * The baseline is stated once, in the Introduction, with 13.7 as its home.
  * 3.3 is removed. Its content moved to 11.3 and Extension Points, and nothing renumbers.
  * Binding cross-references now point to 5.5.2.
  * Privacy no longer uses "delivery" or "renewals".
* **One home per rule:**
  * tenant selection in 3.2;
  * retrieval outcomes in 5.3, including the size bound, with registration now citing 5.3;
  * duplicate member names in 5.2.
* **Sentence-level:**
  * `client_id` rejection in one sentence;
  * the 5.6 proof bullets untangled;
  * the always-true condition removed;
  * the Admission definition without nested parentheses;
  * "counts for nothing in admission" in place of "admits nothing";
  * "Issuer Trust" as the Section 4 heading.
* **Registration:**
  * a list for `invalid_software_statement`;

pulls.title: Editorial pass on registration before -00
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Full editorial pass on registration before -00. Three cold reviewers produced findings: a working-group reviewer, an implementer who walked six scenarios, and an RFC editor on structure and simplification. I added my own read and triaged everything into one plan. You approved all seven clarifications and the metadata rename, and skipped a new example. Each finding is its own commit, so any can be dropped alone. A cold verifier then checked every commit against its base. Its 11 findings are the last 8 commits. One of them was a restored sentence the restructure had deleted.

## Structure (first commit, moves only)

All three reviewers asked for this independently. No other draft cites registration's sections.

```
3   Consumption at Registration
3.1 Tenant Restriction        (new: the tenant rule and table)
3.2 Public Clients
3.3 Repeated Registration     (with the default policy from old 8.2)
4   Registration Validity     (was 3.2)
5   Requests Under a Registration (was 3.3; tenant MUSTs folded into steps 1 and 4)
6   Renewal                   (was 3.4; gains the PAR-endpoint rule)
7   Error Responses
```

Example and Deployment Considerations also lose their lone subsections.

## Normative changes

* **N1, replacement document rules.** A replacement whose document fails one of Section 3's rules now fails the replacement rules. The failing rules are the digest, CIMD validation, an omitted method, a claimable redirection URI, and refused metadata. Before, that case had no defined outcome at the token or pushed authorization request endpoint. The separate MUST to derive a replacement's metadata goes, because Section 3 and the atomic update already carry it.
* **N2, required-issuer scope.** The rule now applies to statement-governed registrations whose governing statement's `sub` falls within a covered namespace. "Any registration" read as reaching registrations made without a statement, which record no `sub`.
* **N3 and N7, repeated registration.** A request is repeated if its statement has the `iss` and `sub` of the governing statement of an existing statement-governed registration that is not restricted to another tenant, including one that has ceased to be valid. In a tenant that requires a tenant-scoped decision, the registration must be restricted to that tenant. The outcome depends on the registration repeated: local policy for a confidential-client registration, and a MUST NOT create for a public-client registration.
  * Public-client outcomes are now a table keyed by `iss` and `jti`: the governing statement gets the existing registration, a later one is evaluated as a delivery, and any other with an `iat` no later than the governing statement's is rejected.
  * The earlier-`iat` rejection now carries the usable-tenant condition. Before, a request in another tenant was both rejected and a new registration.
  * A policy rejection uses `unapproved_software_statement`.
  * The default policy is one registration per `iss` and `sub`, per tenant.
* **N4, PAR endpoint.** One condition: every grant the registration permits needs an authorization request or a refresh token. The old gloss contradicted it for token exchange.
* **N5, ceasing to be valid.** A registration ceasing to be valid does not expire its credentials, including the registration access token. Otherwise restoring through RFC 7592 would be impossible. It also does not by itself revoke access tokens already issued.
* **N6, step 3.** A delivered statement is classified by its claims before it is validated. A replacement applied at step 3 stands even if a later step or the grant rejects the request.
* **Tenant rules.** The tenant rules of steps 1 and 4 now explicitly reach every request under a registration, including RFC 7592 read and delete requests. Before, the paragraph that moved said this.
* **Metadata rename.** `software_statement_registration_validity_supported` becomes `software_statement_registration_supported`. No other draft or artifact uses the name.
* **Client MAY removed.** "A request MAY carry metadata" becomes "Metadata in a registration or update request is ignored".
* **Keyword census.** MUST goes from 28 to 26 and MAY from 2 to 1.
  * The two MUSTs removed are the derive-replacement MUST and the duplicate-names MUST, which core 5.2 now covers for any server resolving a reviewed document.
  * The two tenant MUSTs moved into steps 1 and 4 unchanged.

## Editorial

* **Security rationale corrected.** An omitted authentication method is refused because nobody reviewed it. The old text said it would "issue a client secret to any holder", which is equally true of a declared shared-secret method. 11.1 now says that plainly.
* **11.2** says when a narrower review takes effect.
* **Definitions.** "Replacement" is defined, Governing Statement carries its `iss` and `jti` identity, and the delivery table applies its first matching row.
* **One name per state.** "Ceases to be valid" replaces five variants, and "octets" replaces "bytes".
* **Restatements cut:** the Public Clients introduction, the delivery paragraph's rule for registrations outside this specification, the update-request explanation, "including its audience", and the citation of an establishment rule for registrations.
* **Error section.** `invalid_software_statement` is split, "well formed" replaces "valid", and the size bound is folded into "cannot be obtained". The other-endpoints form is rewritten.
* **Acknowledgments** dropped. 11.3 now says "new client identifier URL" instead of "new identity".
* **RFC 7592 stays informative.** Making it normative is an idnits downref error, because it is Experimental and not in the Downref Registry. That commit was reverted.

## Deferred to -01

* Whether a server-assigned `client_id` may equal the CIMD URL, which would make a delivery indistinguishable from a runtime presentation.
* A replacement at the token endpoint switching to an authentication method that needs a credential the registration lacks.
* Rejecting a public-client document that lists other grants.

## Verification

* Registration shrinks from 5,027 to 4,948 words.
* All five drafts build, and each draft's idnits counts are unchanged.
* No rendered line is over 72 columns, there are no em dashes, and `git diff --check` is clean.
* The anchors `registration-default` and `renewal-cadence` were removed, and neither had remaining citations. `tenant-restriction` was added.
* ID-JAG -06 was published today. It still defines `aud_tenant` (Section 3.1) and registers it (Section 11.5), and the local reference cache was refreshed. Core is unchanged in this PR.

## Verifier fixes (last five commits)

pulls.title: Family review, PR B: lifecycle, attested, issuance, MCP, README (stacked on #120)
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
PR B of the family review: lifecycle, attested, issuance, the MCP profile, and the README. **Stacked on #120 (PR A)**: merge #120 first. This PR's commits then fast-forward onto main. One editor agent per draft applied the approved findings, one commit each, in separate worktrees. I applied the MCP and README fixes. Four cold verifier passes then checked every commit, and their findings are the last 23 commits. The attested editor's two flagged downgrades were restored before verification.

## Approved normative changes

* **MCP profile matches the core and lifecycle:**
  * A public client's statement presented at the token endpoint is rejected (core 5.6.2); only a pulled one is review-only.
  * The diagram binds the presenter to the document key or a DPoP key.
  * Withdrawal ends refresh unless a later statement replaces it.
  * A presented statement under a refusal record is rejected, now stated outside the review-only list.
* **Lifecycle:**
  * Pull selection ignores statements a refusal record covers.

* **Attested:**

* **Issuance:**

| Attested | 28 to 20 | 93 to 69 | 3 | 6 to 4 |

pulls.title: Make core independent of its companion drafts
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Core cited the registration draft 12 times and the lifecycle draft 11 times. The `LIFECYCLE` reference targets an editor's copy on GitHub Pages, and lifecycle is not being submitted, so a -00 would cite a document that nobody can cite. This PR makes core read on its own before the -00 submission.

1. **Make core's extension hooks generic (`dc42264`).**
   * Section 5.4: `software_statement` is consumed "as a runtime presentation or in a role defined by an extension the server implements". On refresh under an establishment, "a server ignores the parameter unless an extension it implements defines its role there". This stays a separate sentence ahead of "any other role is rejected", so a core-only server still ignores a lifecycle replacement rather than rejecting it.
   * Section 3: the rule rejecting a statement in an RFC 7591 registration request now excepts a server where "an extension it implements defines consumption of the statement at registration ({{extensions}})". The author chose generic wording over citing the registration draft.

Core 11.3's counting of registrations, with its exemption for a registration under which no access token has been issued, now lives in registration's Repeated Registration. pulls.title: Move the registration-time required-issuer rule into registration
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Follows #123. Core's Admission definition covered "a request or a registration". That definition was the only way core Section 4's required-issuer rule reached registration creation: the server "MUST NOT admit software in a covered namespace in that tenant without a current statement from the required issuer". The registration draft's own required-issuer rule rejects requests under an existing registration, not its creation. This PR gives registration its own rule, then narrows core's definition, so core no longer mentions registrations in its definitions.

## Commits

1. **Apply the required issuer when creating a registration (`39c1d2b`).** Registration Section 3 now says: "If a required issuer covers the statement's `sub` in the request's tenant (Section 4 of {{STATEMENT}}), the authorization server MUST NOT create a registration on a statement from another issuer." The rule says "create", so it leaves renewal unchanged: a replacement must already carry the governing statement's issuer. The `unapproved_software_statement` entry gains this case, since no code covered it before.
2. **Limit core's Admission definition to requests (`e27ed91`).** Admission is now "acceptance of a client for a request". Registration's sentence "the registration is the admission" would have stretched core's narrowed term. It now reads "registration has no review-only form, so a condition that would make a presentation review-only rejects the registration."

## Normative changes

* **Moved:** one MUST NOT. Registration gains it, so its MUST NOT count goes from 5 to 6. Core's keyword sequence is unchanged, and the rule it implied for registrations through the definition now lives in registration.
* **Error code:** `unapproved_software_statement` now names the required-issuer case, scoped to a registration Section 3 forbids creating. An RFC 7592 update delivering a replacement from another issuer keeps `invalid_software_statement`.
* **Still open for -01:** whether a required issuer blocks a registration made without any statement. Core's old wording only arguably covered it, and neither draft claims it now.

## Checks

* All drafts build.
* Core keyword sequence identical; registration adds exactly the one sentence above. No lost anchors or unresolved citations, and no keyword sentence newly opens a paragraph.
* No rendered line over 72 columns, no table rows leaking into prose, no em dashes, and `git diff --check` is clean.
* idnits counts unchanged: core 4 warnings and 2 comments, registration 3 warnings and 2 comments.

## Review fixes

* `f3a6476`: the new error-code case had been written as a property of the statement, so it also matched an RFC 7592 update delivering a replacement from issuer B after the tenant came to require issuer A. That update is already assigned `invalid_software_statement`. The case is now scoped to a registration that Section 3 forbids creating.

pulls.title: Required-issuer scope for registrations; lifecycle replacement metadata

pulls.body:

2. **Advertise refresh replacement in server metadata (`4d92eb4`, lifecycle and attested).** Core has a server that implements no extension ignore a statement offered on refresh. So a successful refresh doesn't show that a replacement was applied, and CIMD clients reach servers with no prior relationship.

For refresh under an establishment, it says that a client needing a later review to govern the grant at a server not advertising `true` opens a new grant by runtime presentation. The value does not describe registration renewal, which a registration-only server can perform on refresh.
   * The value is registered in the IANA "OAuth Authorization Server Metadata" registry.
   * Lifecycle's later sections renumber: Security becomes 12 and Privacy 13. The attested draft's two citations of them are updated.

## Normative changes

* **Registration:** no new keyword. The added sentence restates, for this case, the `unapproved_software_statement` assignment Section 7 already makes. Scope clarification.
* **Lifecycle:** one new OPTIONAL metadata value and its IANA registration.
* **Attested:** citation renumbering only.

## Checks

* All five drafts build.

  * registration and attested keep identical keyword sequences;

pulls.body:
Resolves every item deferred from #126, following the latest review's guidance where it gave any. There are ten commits, one per item. Core and registration are touched editorially only, so the -00 tag waits for this PR.

## Requirement changes (lifecycle, issuance)

1. **Lifecycle must advertise replacement support (`Require lifecycle servers to advertise replacement support`).**
   * Section 9 adds: "An authorization server implementing this specification MUST publish `software_statement_replacement_supported` with the value `true`."
   * The flag keeps its capability-specific meaning, and its default stays `false` when omitted.
   * Attested's metadata section points to the requirement ("As a server implementing {{LIFECYCLE}}, it also publishes ...") rather than repeating the MUST.
2. **Wrong client versus wrong replacement on refresh (`Distinguish a wrong client from a wrong replacement on refresh`).** A refresh used to get `statement_required` whenever `client_id` differed from the replacement's `sub`. Now:
   * a `client_id` that is not the client the refresh token was issued to fails the grant binding and gets `invalid_grant` (Section 5.2 of RFC 6749);
   * a replacement naming another `sub` than that `client_id` keeps `statement_required`;
   * RFC 6749 is added to lifecycle's normative references.
3. **An issuer relying on its own record (`Except header checks when an issuer relies on its record`).** Issuance Section 11 required "every check" of core 3.2 and 5.1, but a record has no JOSE header or signature, and only the signature check was excepted. The MUST now excepts "the checks of its JOSE header and signature". The runtime sentence now only says where the record takes the statement's place.

## Clarifications (core, registration)

4. **Core 5.3 (`Name every retrieval the request forgery rule covers`).** The sentence on request forgery protections now also names "a statement key set or the issuer metadata that locates one". It already applied the policy "to every referenced location"; now its list agrees with that MUST. No keyword changed.
5. **Core 5.6.3 (`Attach the audit pointer to what it covers`).** The `{{ui-audit}}` pointer moves to "though it can record the statement's issuer for audit", which that section covers.
6. **Registration's Replacement definition (`Cover repeated registration in the Replacement definition`).** It now covers a statement "delivered under the registration or carried in a repeated public-client registration request", which Repeated Registration already evaluates as a replacement.

## MCP profile

7. **Claimable redirects (`Cover every claimable redirect in the MCP profile`).** Sections 3.3, 4.4 and 8.2 name any redirection URI another application on the same device could claim, including a private-use URI scheme, not only loopback.
8. **Pulls at the pushed authorization request endpoint (`Pull at the pushed authorization request endpoint in MCP`).** Section 4.1 lists the pushed authorization request endpoint, as the core does.
9. **Example audience (`Explain the MCP example's missing audience`).** The 7.2 caption no longer justifies the missing `aud` as a catalog listing. It states the consequence, and says a catalog that knows its servers names them, as core 12.2 recommends. The JSON is unchanged.
10. **Servers that don't accept presentation (`Say what an MCP server that accepts no presentation does`).** Section 4.1, which makes accepting presented statements a MAY, now says a server that declines ignores the parameter and processes the request as one presenting no statement. Sections 3.4 and 6 point there instead of describing behavior the core doesn't define.

The Token Status List citations were rechecked by the reviewer against -21 (Sections 6.2, 8.3 and 13.7). No change.

* noop_check:

* normative_diff matches items 1 to 3 exactly. condition_record flags only item 1's new sentence as a paragraph lead, which is intended: its condition, "implementing this specification", is in the sentence.

* idnits counts unchanged.

## Review fixes

Section 4.1 also says such a server still rejects the parameter in any role the core does not permit, such as code redemption, and that a server implementing lifecycle processes a replacement offered on refresh.

pulls.title: Pre-00 fixes from the issue review
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Four small fixes from the issue review, applied before the core and registration -00 submission.

## Commits

1. **Advise against registration use in published statements (registration 11.1, #47 item 2).** Anyone can read a statement a client publishes at its `software_statements_uri`. Registration now says an issuer ought not to permit registration in such a statement. Core is already safe by default, since a statement without `statement_uses` permits presentation only.
2. **Point issuers at the CIMD document size limit (core 11.2, #49).** Section 8.7 of CIMD recommends that a server read at most 5 kilobytes, so an issuer ought not to issue a statement over a larger document.
3. **Cite base64url and duplicate member names (core 3.1 and 5.2, #51 last item).** The metadata digest cites Section 2 of RFC 7515 for base64url without padding. The duplicate member name rule cites Section 4 of RFC 8259, which is added as a normative reference.
4. **Do not assign the CIMD URL as a registered client_id (registration 3, #131 item 1).** Adds: "The authorization server MUST NOT assign that URL as the registered `client_id`, which would make a request carrying it ambiguous between the registration and the CIMD client the URL identifies ({{CIMD}})."

## Normative changes

* Registration gains one MUST NOT (commit 4). Its MUST NOT count goes from 6 to 7.
* Core's keyword sequence is identical. The duplicate member name MUST gains only a citation.
* Commits 1 and 2 are "ought not to" guidance.

* noop_check on both drafts: no anchors lost and no unresolved citations.
